messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was twenty-one when it happened, a junior urban planner walking home through a part of the city where redevelopment had stalled — empty lots, a few boarded storefronts, and the sharp smell of cheap liquor from a crowd gathered outside a corner store. He had looked down at his phone for a moment, and when he looked up, one of the men had yelled something, and then a bottle was flying toward his face. He didn't see it connect, only felt the explosion of pain and the shock of his own blood. What he remembered later — and what he still could not shake — were not minutes or a sequence, but three snapshots: the arc of the bottle against the streetlight, the wet sound of glass on his cheekbone, and the face of a bystander staring at him without moving to help. The police came eventually, but they took a report without interest, and he never heard back. That silence lodged itself as certainty: the people who should have protected him had let him down, and nothing he could do would stop bad things from happening.

Now, two years later, Kwame worked in a community planning office where public meetings were part of the job. He could not afford to be afraid of people expressing anger — but he was. Even calm disagreement from a colleague made his chest tighten, because the tone of raised voices, no matter the subject, pulled him straight back into that alley. The smell of someone's beer at a networking event would flood him with the same visceral startle: his head would whip around, his shoulders would lift, and he would feel ready to run even while knowing, rationally, that he was indoors and surrounded by professionals. After the first few times that happened, he quietly stopped going to any event where drinks were served, telling himself it wasn't worth the risk — but the avoidance only made those situations feel more dangerous in his mind. Soon, even the smell of beer from a passing stranger on the street became a trigger, because his mind had learned to pair that sensory cue with the fact that he had to avoid it. Ordinary sounds — a dropped binder, a chair scraping — triggered the same jolt. He found it impossible to believe anyone who told him he was safe. Every raised voice he heard at work told him, with a certainty he couldn't argue with, that he could not handle even the smallest confrontation without falling apart.

The bottle-throwing had been a single moment, but that moment kept returning as a series of still images that overwhelmed him so completely he had to stop whatever he was doing, pressing his palms against his desk until his heartbeat slowed. To push the images away, he began opening a poker app on his phone whenever they surfaced, finding that the concentration required to play a hand gave his mind something else to grip. He knew what had happened, but when he tried to tell anyone — a therapist he saw once, a coworker who asked — he could not find words for it. The pictures came without language, and the failure to describe them only reinforced his sense that he could not cope with even the slightest upset. Because those images intruded so vividly and without warning, he began to see echoes of the assault in everyday sounds — a door slamming, a glass being set down — each one becoming a new trigger he hadn't anticipated. That helplessness made him watchful. Every unexpected movement in his peripheral vision felt like a threat, and every small sound rekindled the memory, so that the loop tightened: the memory triggered more hypervigilance, the hypervigilance made him jump at a colleague's sudden step, and that startle returned him to the snapshot of the bottle's arc. Already running on that level of threat, he noticed that even neutral things — a car backfiring, a colleague raising a hand to wave — now felt like warnings he couldn't afford to ignore. Living in that state of constant threat, he found that avoiding people he didn't fully trust was the only way to keep the fear manageable, and gambling online became a brief escape when the vigilance became unbearable.

He had developed strategies that made sense to him at the time. He avoided any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation — he stopped going to happy hours, he emailed instead of speaking in meetings, he let his opinions slide when a project lead pressed back. Each time he let a point go unchallenged, he felt a quiet certainty hardening: that he was weaker than everyone else in the room, that the assault had shrunk him to someone who could no longer speak. Each person he avoided, each meeting he stayed silent in, became a fresh reminder of what had happened — the avoidance itself had begun to carve a map of the event into his daily life, and every detour he took reinforced the memory. The self-blame was constant: he dwelled on what he had done wrong, walking down that street, not crossing earlier, not seeing the group. To interrupt the rumination, he began gambling — online poker, small stakes, mostly — because the rush of a hand felt like control, even if it only lasted a minute. But never having stayed in a situation long enough to learn it might be safe, his body had no evidence that the danger had passed — the avoidance and the gambling sealed that possibility off, and the sense of threat only grew. But the gambling brought its own consequences: after a loss he would replay the assault again, blaming himself for the bet the same way he blamed himself for the alley, and the cycle fed itself. The avoidance left him isolated at work; a colleague remarked that he seemed distant, and he could not explain why.

The deepest turning point came during a public hearing on a rezoning project. A resident raised his voice, gesturing with a rolled-up map in his hand. Kwame's vision tunnelled; he saw the bottle, not the map, and before he could stop himself he had left the room, shaking, unable to speak. His supervisor called the next day, concerned. That was the conversation that brought him to the clinic. What he feared most was that the feeling of institutional failure would prove true — that even help would let him down. But he was also terrified that he would never stop watching for the next thrown object, and that the only thing he could still control, the gambling, was taking everything else away.
